items.question: Why is everything established as pure in the teaching of the Vīrāvali?
premises: Everything that has attained identity with consciousness is pure.
This is stated in the glorious Vīrāvali.
The Vīrāvali teaches the discernment of pure and impure.
items.inference: Because all things share identity with consciousness, they are established as pure in the Vīrāvali's discernment.
uncertainties: The exact text referred to as śrīmadvīrāvalau is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: All things that have attained identity with consciousness are therefore established as pure. This is said in the glorious Vīrāvali, in its teaching on the discernment of purity and impurity.

items.question: What is the true criterion for calling something impure?
premises: There is no carrier of all things that is itself lifeless.
Nothing exists as something entirely without life.
Whatever is devoid of life is to be known as impure.
items.inference: Impurity is defined by the absence of life or consciousness, not by material form alone.
uncertainties: The sense of jīva here may range from biological life to conscious presence.
items.plain_english: There is no lifeless carrier of all things; nothing is truly without life. Know that whatever is devoid of life is impure.

items.question: How can purity be attained in relation to consciousness?
premises: Whatever is not far from consciousness can bring purity.
A non-conceptual state supports this nearness to consciousness.
Sages also became pure in this way.
items.inference: Purity arises by abiding in a non-conceptual state close to consciousness, as exemplified by the sages.
uncertainties: The exact scope of avikalpa here may include both absence of discursive thought and direct awareness.
items.plain_english: Therefore, whatever is not far from consciousness can bring purity. Even the sages became pure by abiding in a non-conceptual state.

items.question: Why was the distinction of purity and impurity concealed by the sages?
premises: The sages concealed that principle for the protection of the world.
Purity and impurity may appear in external things.
They are not objective properties of things like the color blue.
items.inference: The sages concealed the deeper principle because purity and impurity are not inherent in external objects but depend on another basis.
uncertainties: The referent of tattattva may be the ultimate principle or the specific teaching about purity.
items.plain_english: For the protection of the world, the sages carefully concealed that principle. Even when purity and impurity seem to appear in external things, they are not fixed properties of those things like blueness is.

items.question: Is purity or impurity a property of the knower or of the object?
premises: Purity and impurity arise from experiencing unity or non-unity with consciousness.
This makes them primarily properties of the knower.
Even if treated as properties of objects, they depend on a limiting measure.
items.inference: Purity and impurity belong to the knower's relation to consciousness, and any object-based account still depends on that relation.
uncertainties: mātrā may refer to a limiting measure, standpoint, or cognitive frame.
items.plain_english: This distinction is really a property of the knower, arising from the experience of unity or non-unity with consciousness. Even if one treats it as a property of objects, it still depends on a limiting standpoint.

items.question: How does ritual usage show that purity rules are not absolute?
premises: In the Sautramani rite, liquor is treated as pure for the Hotr priest.
What is pure in that context may be reversed for another.
This shows that injunctions can contradict one another, even within their own scriptural statements.
items.inference: Ritual examples demonstrate that purity and impurity are context-dependent and that injunctions do not have absolute, uniform force.
uncertainties: The exact ritual details behind śuddhānyasya are compressed in the verse.
items.plain_english: In the Sautramani rite, liquor is considered pure for the Hotr priest, while for another the valuation is reversed. This shows that injunctions can contradict one another, even by their own statements.

items.question: Are scriptural rules about purity applied uniformly or through reasoning?
premises: Scripture sometimes presents conflicting injunction and prohibition, as in the case of killing a brahmin.
Rules about food and similar matters are also handled in this way.
Such rules are practiced by relying on reasoning.
items.inference: Scriptural rules concerning purity and conduct are not mechanically uniform but are applied through contextual reasoning.
uncertainties: The specific example of brahmahatyā injunction and prohibition is alluded to, not explained.
items.plain_english: This is sometimes shown, as with the conflicting injunction and prohibition regarding the killing of a brahmin. Rules about food and similar matters are also practiced by relying on reasoning.

items.question: What scriptural authority supports the hierarchy of teachings?
premises: The Great Lord speaks at the beginning of the Sarvajnanottara.
He refers to teachings spoken by humans, sages, gods, Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, and others.
This places those teachings within a broader revealed hierarchy.
items.inference: The Sarvajnanottara presents a hierarchy of teachings issued through various divine and human speakers under the Great Lord's authority.
uncertainties: The exact quotation from Sarvajnanottara is only summarized here.
items.plain_english: At the beginning of the Sarvajnanottara, the Great Lord speaks of what has been declared by humans, sages, gods, Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, and others.

items.question: Can a lower scriptural teaching override a higher one?
premises: Teachings have successively higher levels of excellence.
A higher teaching overrides an earlier or lower one.
The Shaiva teaching is presented as higher in this hierarchy.
items.inference: Because higher teachings override lower ones, the Shaiva teaching cannot be overruled by Vaishnava statements.
uncertainties: The verse assumes a shared acceptance of the scriptural hierarchy it asserts.
items.plain_english: Because each higher teaching surpasses the earlier one and overrides it, the Shaiva teaching can never be overruled by Vaishnava statements.

rows.grounds: brahma (Brahma) + saṃbhūta (born from) + na (not) + iti (thus) + ādi (and so on)

items.question: What is the consequence of reversing the proper hierarchy of teachings?
premises: One should not dismiss the Vaishnava teaching by appealing to teachings born from Brahma and so on.
A person who overrules teachings in reverse order is deluded.
Such reversal leads to a share in sin.
items.inference: Respecting the proper hierarchy of teachings is necessary, and reversing it through delusion brings moral fault.
uncertainties: The compressed phrase brahmasaṃbhūtairnetyādi leaves the exact contrasted teachings implicit.
items.plain_english: One should not examine or dismiss the Vaishnava teaching by appealing to teachings that arise from Brahma and the like. Whoever, deluded by reversal, overrules them in the wrong order becomes a sharer in sin.

items.question: Which duties should a practitioner primarily follow?
premises: Worldly duties are not to be taken as primary.
Duties prescribed by other scriptures are not to be followed as one's main path.
One should practice what is declared in one's own stream.
items.inference: The practitioner should primarily follow the discipline of their own tradition rather than worldly or external scriptural prescriptions.
uncertainties: The degree to which other prescriptions are excluded versus subordinated is not fully explicit.
items.plain_english: Therefore, O Skanda, one should not primarily follow worldly duties, nor what is prescribed by other scriptures. One should practice what is declared in one's own tradition.

items.question: Why does divine origin not make all scriptures equally binding in the same way?
premises: Even the Veda and other teachings were established by the Lord.
Nevertheless, they differ according to contraction, presence, absence, and alternative framing.
Their applicability varies with the condition of those they address.
items.inference: Although all such teachings may have divine origin, their scope and binding force differ according to levels of contraction and capacity.
uncertainties: The compound saṃkocabhāvābhāvavikalpataḥ is compressed and allows more than one technical unpacking.
items.plain_english: Although even the Veda and other teachings were established by the Lord, they still operate according to differences of contraction, presence, absence, and alternative application. For that reason, their force is not the same for everyone.
